content: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a medical condition characterized by necrosis of tissue, leading to the formation of deep ulcers. These ulcers most commonly appear on the legs. When they develop, they can result in chronic wounds. Initially, the ulcers may resemble small insect bites or papules, but they progressively enlarge into more significant lesions. Although these wounds rarely result in mortality, they can cause significant pain and scarring. The condition was first identified in 1930 and affects approximately 1 in 100,000 individuals. While it can occur at any age, it predominantly affects individuals in their 40s and 50s. There are two primary forms of pyoderma gangrenosum. The first is the classic ulcerative form, which typically occurs on the legs. The second is an atypical form, which is more superficial and often affects the hands or other parts of the body. Additional variations of the disease include peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum (accounting for 15% of all cases), bullous pyoderma gangrenosum, pustular pyoderma gangrenosum, and vegetative pyoderma gangrenosum. The exact cause of pyoderma gangrenosum is not well understood. However, it is believed to result from immune system dysfunction, particularly involving abnormal neutrophil activity. At least half of the individuals with pyoderma gangrenosum also have systemic illnesses that impair their overall health. Examples of such associated conditions include ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple myeloma. Physical examination of the extremities often reveals characteristic lesions of pyoderma gangrenosum. These findings are well-documented in dermatological atlases. Pyoderma gangrenosum is frequently associated with other medical conditions. Commonly linked disorders include inflammatory bowel diseases such as chronic ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. It is also associated with various forms of arthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis and seronegative symmetrical polyarthritis. Hematological diseases linked to pyoderma gangrenosum include myelocytic leukemia, hairy cell leukemia, myelofibrosis, myeloid metaplasia, and monoclonal gammopathy (IgA). A range of treatment options is available for managing pyoderma gangrenosum.
